title: Create Account: Local Account
summary: Local account creation is a persistence behaviour in which an intruder with sufficient rights adds a user account that exists only on one machine or device, so future access needs no malware to remain installed. On Windows the built in account management command can add a user and then place it in a privileged local group, on Linux the user creation utility does the same, on macOS the directory services command line tool can create the entry, and appliances, ESXi hosts and Kubernetes clusters each offer their own account interfaces. Because the account is local, it is invisible in domain group reports and the attacker can later authenticate over remote desktop, SMB or a management interface with a plausible name. The telemetry is specific: Windows records account creation and group membership changes in the security log, with new account events and privileged group additions being the classic pair, and each new account also produces a first logon far from any change record. Legitimate service provisioning and support procedures create accounts too, so the reliable test is whether a change record exists and whether the account name and privileges match a real business function.

beginner.definition: A local account is a user account that lives on one single computer or device, not in a central directory. This sub-technique is when an attacker creates such an account so they can log in again later. It works even if every malicious file is removed.
beginner.whyItMatters: Attackers like accounts because accounts are not files. Antivirus tools do not delete them and they survive cleanup of malware. The login uses normal credentials, so nothing looks broken. Many organisations also forget to review accounts that exist on only one machine.
howItWorks: The attacker gains administrator rights on a single computer or device.
They add a new user with a built in tool, such as net user add on Windows.
The new account is then added to a privileged group, giving it strong rights.
On other systems the local tools differ, for example useradd on Linux hosts.
Network devices, virtual hosts and container platforms each have their own account commands.
Later the attacker logs in over a remote service using that account and its password.
beginner.example: Think of a shared flat with one front door. A guest with a copy of the landlord key cuts a new key for themselves and hides it outside. Even if the guest is asked to leave and their bags are searched, the new key still opens the door. Nobody changed the lock, so the flat looks exactly as it did before.
takeaways: Accounts are a form of persistence that survives removing malware from the machine.
Watch for new account events and for new accounts added to privileged local groups.
Review privileged local accounts on hosts and devices, not only in the central directory.

objectives: Explain what a local account is and why it is useful for persistence.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from its parent and from domain or cloud accounts.
Recognise the account creation and group membership events recorded on a Windows host.
List at least three platforms, beyond Windows, where local accounts can be created.
Explain why an account can survive the removal of the malware that created it.
